passage: I'm Jeevan. When Yogesh joined our class in June, his hair was oiled flat, his shirt was tucked right up under his chest, and he stood up every time Sir came in, even when nobody else did. Some boys smirked. By July his hair was dry and messy like everyone's, and his shirt was only half tucked at the back. He had stopped standing up; he just straightened in his seat like the rest of us. He also started saying "bro" the way Manish does. I don't know if he likes it or just doesn't want the smirks.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do every time Sir came in during June?
qa.a: He stood up, even when nobody else did.

qa.q: Why might Yogesh have changed his hair and shirt by July?
qa.a: He probably felt self-conscious about the smirks and wanted to fit in with how the class looked and acted.

qa.q: How could a classmate like Jeevan make it easier for a new student?
qa.a: Talk to him and let him know he doesn't have to copy everything to be accepted.

qa.q: What does Jeevan admit he cannot know?
qa.a: Whether Yogesh actually likes the changes or is only avoiding the smirks.

grounding: It shows, from a classmate's view, a new boy picking up and following the class's unwritten rules on dress and behaviour.

passage:
Week one: Everyone in Class 7 started wearing their socks pushed down to the ankle. Darshan, twelve, kept his pulled up to the knee, the way his mother liked. Gurleen whispered, "Nobody does that anymore."
Week two: Darshan rolled his socks down on the bus and pulled them up again before reaching home. His stomach felt tight both times.
Week four: He asked his mother, "Can I wear them low? Everyone does." She said the school rule was only "clean socks." He wore them low openly. Then he noticed Gurleen had a bright new hair clip, and within days half the girls had one.

qa.q: How did Darshan wear his socks in week one?
qa.a: Pulled up to the knee, the way his mother liked.

qa.q: What does Darshan's tight stomach in week two suggest?
qa.a: He felt uneasy hiding the change from his mother while also worrying about standing out at school.

qa.q: Which choice worked better for Darshan, and why?
qa.a: Asking his mother openly worked better than secretly rolling his socks, because it ended the hiding and the tight feeling.

qa.q: How does Gurleen seem to see these trends?
qa.a: She pays close attention to what's in, pointing out his socks and later starting a trend herself.

grounding: It shows a boy noticing and adopting an unwritten dress trend over several weeks.

passage: Akash, I remember my first week at boarding school in Shillong. I was nine, the new girl, Elizabeth. Nobody told me the rules, but I learned them fast. The older girls never ran in the corridor, even when late; they walked quickly with stiff arms. Everyone rolled their cardigan sleeves twice, not once. And at dinner you waited for the head girl to lift her spoon. On the second night I lifted mine first. Twenty faces turned. I put it down so fast it clattered. By the end of the month I was rolling my sleeves twice without thinking. Only years later did I wonder who had made those rules at all.

qa.q: How many times did the girls roll their cardigan sleeves?
qa.a: They rolled them twice, not once.

qa.q: What was young Elizabeth feeling when twenty faces turned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, realising she had broken a rule nobody had said aloud.

qa.q: How could an older girl have helped a newcomer like Elizabeth?
qa.a: Quietly explain the customs in the first week, so she didn't have to learn them by being stared at.

qa.q: How does the grown-up Elizabeth see those rules now?
qa.a: She wonders who made them at all, suggesting she now sees them as habits rather than real rules.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a nine-year-old learning and following a hostel's unspoken rules.

passage: On the first day back at school, Jagdish saw it at once: every boy in Class 6 wore short ankle socks. His were long, pulled up to the knee. Someone giggled. At home he asked Sonali, his mother, for new socks. She looked at the money tin. 'Next month, beta.' That night Jagdish sat on his bed, folding his long socks down twice, then three times, until they looked short. The next morning he checked his feet in the mirror and walked in a little taller.

qa.q: How did Jagdish make his long socks look short?
qa.a: He folded them down several times until they looked short.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish want short socks so badly?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed when someone giggled at his long socks, and he wanted to fit in with the other boys.

qa.q: What could Sonali say that might help Jagdish?
qa.a: She could acknowledge how much fitting in matters to him and praise his clever solution while money is tight.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when she sees the folded socks?
qa.a: She may feel touched by his effort and a little sad that she could not buy new ones yet.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing and adapting to an unwritten dress norm among peers, under money constraints.

passage: In her Hyderabad school, Rashmi noticed that nobody in Class 5 carried a cartoon water bottle any more. They all had plain steel ones. Her bottle had a big pink rabbit. At lunch she kept it under the desk. Her cousin Suraj, in Class 7, laughed when she told him. 'There are rules nobody says out loud. Like, you don't run to the canteen. You walk fast.' Rashmi thought about it. The next day she walked fast, not ran, and asked Amma if she could use Appa's old steel bottle.

qa.q: What was on Rashmi's water bottle?
qa.a: It had a big pink rabbit.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi keep her bottle under the desk?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because it didn't match the unspoken trend, and she didn't want others to notice.

qa.q: What would you advise Rashmi about following these rules?
qa.a: It's okay to follow small trends if she likes, but she should also know she can keep things she loves without shame.

qa.q: How does Suraj see these unwritten school rules?
qa.a: He sees them as normal and a bit funny, something older kids simply know and follow.

grounding: Shows a child recognising and adapting to unwritten peer norms about belongings and behaviour.

passage:
"Didi, pull my socks down more."
Bidisha looked up from her phone. "Why? They're fine."
"Nobody wears them up. Only babies."
"Who said?"
"Nobody said. Everyone just knows." Shankar, eleven, scrunched them down to his ankles. "And I need the side-parting haircut."
"You liked your spikes last month."
"That was last month."
"And your steel tiffin?"
"I'll eat in the corridor. Only I have a steel one."
Bidisha put her phone down. "You know you're allowed to be different?"
"I know," Shankar said, fixing his socks again. "But not yet."

qa.q: How did Shankar want his socks?
qa.a: Pulled down to his ankles.

qa.q: Why did Shankar say "Nobody said. Everyone just knows"?
qa.a: He felt anxious to fit in, following rules no one says out loud but everyone seems to follow.

qa.q: What could Bidisha say to help Shankar balance fitting in and being himself?
qa.a: She could say that small changes are fine, but his steel tiffin or old hairstyle don't make him less liked.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see Shankar's worries?
qa.a: She finds them a bit silly at first, then starts to take them seriously.

grounding: Shows a child noticing and following unspoken rules about dress and style at school.

passage: I'm Arohi. When I started Class 6, I raised my hand for every question, like I always had. By the second week I noticed nobody else did. The girls at the back rolled their eyes, and someone whispered, "Teacher's pet." No one ever said the rule, but I learned it. I started waiting three questions before I raised my hand. Zubin, the boy next to me, never changed. He still asks everything. Sometimes I envy him. Sometimes I think I'm just being smart about it.

qa.q: What did someone whisper about Arohi?
qa.a: "Teacher's pet."

qa.q: How did Arohi feel about Zubin still asking everything?
qa.a: Arohi felt torn: sometimes envious of his freedom, sometimes sure that fitting in was sensible.

qa.q: What would you advise Arohi about raising her hand?
qa.a: Keep asking the questions Arohi really cares about, since learning matters more than a few eye-rolls.

qa.q: What might Zubin feel about the eye-rolling?
qa.a: He may not notice it, or he may simply care more about learning than about fitting in.

grounding: Shows a child recognising an unwritten classroom rule and changing her behaviour to fit it.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Damini, February
Hemant (10) used to bring his toy car to show everyone. This term he's stopped. He now wears three friendship bands like the other boys and asked his mother for the same pencil box everyone has. When I asked about the car, he said, "Nobody brings toys in Class 5." I told him it was fine either way. He's happier in the group, which is good, but he looked sad when I mentioned the car. I'll set up a hobby show so children can share what they like without worry.

qa.q: How many friendship bands does Hemant wear?
qa.a: Three friendship bands.

qa.q: What does Hemant looking sad about the car suggest?
qa.a: He may miss sharing the toy he loved, and feel a pang about giving it up to fit in.

qa.q: Why is Damini's hobby show a good idea?
qa.a: It gives children a safe, approved chance to share what they like without breaking the class's unspoken rules.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother see his request for the same pencil box?
qa.a: She might feel both understanding and a little worried about how much he wants to fit in.

grounding: Shows a child noticing and following classmates' unwritten rules about toys and trends.

passage:
Monday. Ujjwal's diary.
First week at the new school in Class 6, and I figured out the sock rule. Nobody pulls their socks up. They roll them down to the ankle. I pulled mine up like at my old school and Wasim looked at my legs and said, "Bro. Down." Nobody wrote this rule anywhere. There's also a rule that you don't carry your water bottle on your shoulder, you hold it. And lunch boxes are never opened before the second bell. I rolled my socks down in the toilet. I felt stupid for a minute, then kind of relieved, like I'd passed a test nobody told me about.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal roll the socks down?
qa.a: In the toilet.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel after rolling the socks down?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt stupid for a minute, then relieved, as if passing a secret test.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do if one of these rules felt wrong or uncomfortable?
qa.a: Ujjwal could ask a trusted friend like Wasim why the rule exists and decide which ones really matter.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the new student?
qa.a: Wasim probably sees Ujjwal as new and was helping with the unwritten rules in a quick, joking way.

grounding: A child at a new school notices and copies unwritten rules about socks, bottles and lunch.

passage: The fair in Sonepur was two days away, and Aadhya watched the older girls near the water pump. Every one of them had her hair in two braids with red ribbons, and nobody wore a watch on the right wrist. Pooja, who was eleven like Aadhya, had a small cloth bag, not a plastic one. Nobody had said a word about any of this. That night Aadhya asked her mother for red ribbons and moved her watch. At the fair she stood next to Pooja, touching her braid now and then. Pooja smiled. "Nice ribbons." Aadhya let out a breath.

qa.q: How many days away was the fair?
qa.a: Two days away.

qa.q: What does Aadhya letting out a breath when Pooja smiled suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had felt nervous about fitting in and was relieved that her changes were noticed kindly.

qa.q: How could Aadhya's mother talk with her about the ribbons?
qa.a: She could help with the ribbons and also ask what Aadhya herself likes, so fitting in doesn't replace her own choices.

qa.q: How might Pooja see Aadhya's new look?
qa.a: Pooja likely sees it as friendly and nice, and may feel Aadhya is part of the group.

grounding: A small-town girl notices and copies the unwritten dress rules of older girls before a fair.

passage: On his first morning at school in Brisbane, Liam hugged his mum at the gate, the way he always had in Dublin. Behind him, a boy snorted. In class, his new friend Paulo leaned over. "Here, nobody hugs at the gate. You just do a wave, like this." Paulo flicked two fingers. Liam watched for the rest of the day. Everyone wore their hat backwards at lunch, and nobody sat on the top bench. The next morning, Liam gave his mum a small wave at the gate. She looked surprised. On the way in, Paulo nodded at him.

qa.q: What did Paulo tell Liam people do instead of hugging at the gate?
qa.a: A wave, flicking two fingers.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when the boy snorted?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and self-conscious about doing something different.

qa.q: How could Liam's mum support him with the change?
qa.a: She could agree on a private goodbye at home, so he can wave at the gate without losing the hug.

qa.q: How might Liam's mum feel about the small wave?
qa.a: She might feel surprised and a little sad, missing the hug even if she understands.

grounding: A boy at a new school in Australia learns unwritten rules about goodbyes, hats and benches, and changes his behaviour.

passage:
On the first day of Class 6, Vishal, eleven, walked into the classroom and stopped.

Every boy was wearing short ankle socks. His were pulled up to his knees, the way his mother always made him wear them.

Hemant, his friend, whispered, "Fold them down."

"Why?"

"Nobody wears them up anymore."

Vishal looked around. It wasn't a rule. But everyone was doing it. At break, he folded his socks down in the washroom.

That evening, he asked his mother for ankle socks. She sighed. "What's wrong with these?"

"Nothing. They're just not what we wear."

qa.q: How did Vishal's mother make him wear his socks?
qa.a: She always made him wear them pulled up to his knees.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when he noticed everyone's socks?
qa.a: Vishal felt self-conscious and embarrassed, worried about standing out.

qa.q: How could Vishal's mother help him with this?
qa.a: She could listen to why it matters to him and talk about when fitting in is harmless and when it isn't.

qa.q: How might Vishal's mother see his request?
qa.a: She might feel puzzled or a bit frustrated, not seeing what's wrong with the socks.

grounding: A child recognises and adopts an unwritten dress rule about socks at school.

passage:
I'm Thomas, the music teacher. At our Christmas concert rehearsal, Ujjwal, ten, had chosen to sing a slow old carol.

When he started, a few boys at the back giggled. One whispered, "That's so old."

Ujjwal stopped. The next day, he asked to change to the new pop carol everyone else was singing.

I asked him why. He shrugged. "Nobody sings that one anymore."

I'm not sure if he really preferred the new one. He sang it well, but he didn't smile.

qa.q: What did one boy whisper?
qa.a: One whispered, "That's so old."

qa.q: What might Ujjwal have been feeling when he changed his song?
qa.a: Thomas wasn't sure, but Ujjwal may have felt embarrassed and wanted to fit in rather than be laughed at.

qa.q: How could Thomas support Ujjwal?
qa.a: Thomas could talk with Ujjwal privately, say the old carol is lovely, and let Ujjwal choose freely.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Ujjwal's decision?
qa.a: Thomas is unsure whether Ujjwal really preferred the new song, noticing he didn't smile.

grounding: A music teacher observes a child changing his song choice to follow what peers consider acceptable.

passage:
First night of Navratri: Rehana, twelve, joins the garba circle in the society compound and dances her own steps, cutting across the circle. A few girls roll their eyes. She doesn't notice.

Fourth night: Her brother Lalit tells her, "You have to match the circle. And don't cut in." She watches from the side for a while, counting the steps.

Ninth night: Rehana joins the circle at the right moment and matches the clap. An aunty says, "Nice, beta." Rehana grins and spins with everyone.

qa.q: What did Lalit tell Rehana?
qa.a: He told her, "You have to match the circle. And don't cut in."

qa.q: How did Rehana feel on the ninth night?
qa.a: Rehana felt happy and included, grinning as she danced with everyone.

qa.q: What helped Rehana learn the unwritten rules of the garba circle?
qa.a: Lalit's advice and her own watching and counting from the side helped.

qa.q: How might the girls who rolled their eyes see Rehana by the ninth night?
qa.a: They might now accept her, as she follows the circle's rules.

grounding: Over the Navratri nights, a girl learns and follows the unwritten rules of a garba circle.

passage: Leela, your Usha Ammamma was twelve once too, you know. The Onam before I moved to the town school, I wore my old green frock to the class celebration. Every other girl wore a cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait. Nobody said a word, but they stood a little apart from me in the photo. That evening I thought about how they walked, how they folded their hands, who sat where. I asked Amma to alter my cousin's old pavada. On the last day before the holidays I wore it, with jasmine, and Beena waved me into the middle of the line. I felt warm and a little strange, as if I'd learned a password.

qa.q: What did every other girl wear to the class celebration?
qa.a: A cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel when the girls stood apart in the photo?
qa.a: She felt left out and self-conscious, noticing an unspoken rule she hadn't known about.

qa.q: What turning point came that evening, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Usha chose to study the girls' unspoken habits and ask Amma to alter the pavada, which got her waved into the middle of the line.

qa.q: How might Beena have seen Usha on the last day?
qa.a: Beena seems to see Usha as one of the group now, welcoming her into the middle of the line.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing and then following unspoken rules about festival dress, told as a grandmother's memory.
